title: Site HSSE Requirements
summary: The baseline every person working on a forecourt needs: how fuel behaves, the site rules that keep it under control, and what to do when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: How fuel behaves
body: Gasoline (petrol) gives off flammable vapour at very low temperatures. Its flash point is around -43 °C, which means that at any temperature you will ever see in Oman, an open container of petrol is producing vapour that can ignite.

Fuel vapour is heavier than air. It does not rise and disperse; it flows along the ground and collects in low points such as drains, pits, tank sumps and inspection chambers. A source of ignition several metres away from a spill can still ignite it.

Vapour only burns when it is mixed with air within its flammable range. For gasoline this is roughly 1.4 % to 7.6 % by volume. Below the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) the mixture is too lean to burn; above the Upper Explosive Limit (UEL) it is too rich. Gas detectors read in % LEL, so 10 % LEL means the atmosphere is one tenth of the way to being able to burn.
Diesel has a much higher flash point (typically above 55 °C) and is far less volatile, but it still burns fiercely once alight and it makes surfaces dangerously slippery.
keyPoints: Petrol vapour is present at all normal temperatures.
Vapour is heavier than air and collects in low points.
Gas detectors measure flammability as % of the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL).

quiz.prompt: Why is gasoline vapour particularly dangerous around drains and inspection pits?
options: It is heavier than air and collects in low points
It is lighter than air and rises out of them quickly
It reacts chemically with drain water
It only becomes flammable when it is underground
quiz.explanation: Fuel vapour is denser than air, so it flows downhill and pools in drains, pits and sumps where it can travel to an ignition source.

quiz.prompt: A gas detector near a tank lid reads 0 % LEL. What does this mean?
options: The atmosphere is at the most dangerous mixture
No flammable vapour is detected at that point
quiz.explanation: % LEL expresses how close the atmosphere is to the Lower Explosive Limit. 0 % LEL means no flammable gas was detected at the sampling point.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about petrol's flash point is correct?
options: It is about 60 °C, so it is only dangerous in summer
It is the temperature at which petrol boils
It is about -43 °C, so it gives off ignitable vapour at all normal temperatures
quiz.explanation: Petrol's flash point is around -43 °C, far below any ambient temperature, so it constantly produces vapour that can ignite.

quiz.prompt: Gasoline vapour can burn when its concentration in air is between roughly:
quiz.explanation: The flammable range of gasoline vapour is approximately 1.4 % (LEL) to 7.6 % (UEL) by volume in air.

lessons.title: Site rules and PPE
body: Every station enforces a short list of absolute rules. Smoking and naked flames are prohibited anywhere on the site. Engines must be switched off while refuelling. Mobile phones must not be used on the forecourt during fuel deliveries or within the hazardous area around the tanker.

Before starting any work you report to the Station Manager, sign in, and attend a site-specific toolbox talk. You do not start work until the permit for that work has been issued and you have read it.

The work area must be barricaded to separate it from customers and moving vehicles. Use cones and barriers to create an exclusion zone, and agree with the Station Manager which pumps or lanes will be closed.

Minimum PPE on a forecourt is safety footwear and a high-visibility vest. Task-specific PPE is added on top: chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection when handling fuel, flame-resistant (FR) coveralls for work inside hazardous areas, and hearing protection for noisy equipment.
keyPoints: No smoking, no naked flames, engines off.
Sign in, attend the toolbox talk, then start work only under a valid permit.
Minimum PPE: safety footwear + high-visibility vest.

quiz.prompt: You arrive at a station to calibrate a pump. What do you do first?
options: Start work on the pump furthest from customers
Report to the Station Manager and sign in
Barricade the area, then call the Permit Issuer
Call the office to say you have arrived
quiz.explanation: All contractors report to the Station Manager and sign in before anything else, so the site knows who is on it and what work is planned.

quiz.prompt: What is the minimum PPE for anyone working on a forecourt?
options: Safety footwear and a high-visibility vest
No PPE is required for short jobs
quiz.explanation: Safety footwear and a high-visibility vest are the forecourt minimum; task-specific PPE is added according to the JHA.

quiz.prompt: When is mobile phone use restricted on the forecourt?
options: During fuel deliveries and inside the hazardous area around the tanker
quiz.explanation: Ordinary phones are not Ex-rated. They are prohibited around tanker deliveries and in hazardous zones where vapour may be present.

quiz.prompt: Why must the work area be barricaded?
options: To stop the Station Manager entering
Because barriers are required on all permits regardless of task
To separate the work from customers and moving vehicles
quiz.explanation: Barricades create an exclusion zone that protects the public and workers from each other's hazards, especially vehicle traffic.

lessons.title: Spills, fire and evacuation
body: Every forecourt has an Emergency Stop (E-stop) that cuts power to all dispensers at once. Know where it is before you start work. In any fuel emergency, the first action is to activate the E-stop.

For a fuel spill: stop the source if it is safe to do so, eliminate ignition sources, keep people and vehicles away, and contain the spill with the station spill kit. Protect drains first so fuel does not enter the drainage system. Never wash fuel into a drain with water.

For a small fuel fire, use a dry powder or foam extinguisher. Never use water on a fuel fire: it spreads burning liquid. Only fight a fire if you are trained, it is small, and you have a clear escape route behind you.

On the alarm, stop work, make your equipment safe if you can do so immediately, and go to the assembly point. Report to the Station Manager so everyone can be accounted for. Do not return until told it is safe.
keyPoints: E-stop first in any fuel emergency.
Protect drains; never wash fuel away with water.
Dry powder or foam on fuel fires; never water.

quiz.prompt: Fuel is leaking from a dispenser hose. What is the first action?
options: Fetch a hose and wash the fuel away
Take photographs for the incident report
Ask customers to move their cars
quiz.explanation: The E-stop cuts power to all dispensers and stops the flow of fuel. It is always the first action in a forecourt fuel emergency.

quiz.prompt: Which extinguisher should you NOT use on a burning fuel spill?
quiz.explanation: Water spreads burning fuel and can make the fire larger. Use dry powder or foam.

quiz.prompt: When containing a spill, what should you protect first?
quiz.explanation: Fuel entering drains spreads vapour underground and causes pollution. Drain covers or booms go down first.

quiz.prompt: The fire alarm sounds while you are working. After making your work safe, you should:
options: Finish the task quickly before leaving
Leave the site and go home
Go to the assembly point and report to the Station Manager
quiz.explanation: Going to the assembly point and reporting in lets the Station Manager account for everyone on site.

title: Permit to Work
summary: How the Permit to Work system controls non-routine work: who does what, how risk sets the paperwork (WCF and JHA), and how isolation, gas testing and close-out work.

lessons.title: Why we use permits and who signs them
body: A Permit to Work (PTW) is a formal written system used to control work that is non-routine or potentially hazardous. It makes sure the hazards have been thought through, the controls are in place, and everyone involved knows what is happening before work starts.

Typical work that requires a permit on a retail site includes hot work (welding, grinding, cutting), work on or near fuel tanks and lines, confined space entry, excavation, electrical work, and working at height.

Three roles matter. The Permit Holder is the competent person in charge of the work crew; they apply for the permit and make sure the crew follows it. The Permit Issuer reviews the application, verifies conditions and authorises the work. The Station Manager controls the site and must be aware of every live permit.
A permit is only valid for the work, location and time written on it. If any of those change, the permit no longer covers you.
keyPoints: Permits control non-routine and hazardous work.
Permit Holder leads the work; Permit Issuer authorises it.
A permit covers only the stated scope, place and time.

quiz.prompt: Who is responsible for making sure the work crew follows the permit conditions?
quiz.explanation: The Permit Holder leads the crew at the worksite and is accountable for the crew working within the permit.

quiz.prompt: Which of these tasks would normally require a permit on a fuel station?
options: Grinding a bracket near a dispenser
Cleaning the shop windows from the ground
Serving a customer at the counter
quiz.explanation: Grinding is hot work. Hot work on a forecourt is high-risk and always requires a permit.

quiz.prompt: Your permit covers work on Pump 3. The Station Manager asks you to also look at Pump 4. What do you do?
options: Do it, as it is the same type of work
Do it, but note it on the permit afterwards
Stop and get the permit amended or a new permit issued first
Ask a crew member to do it instead
quiz.explanation: A permit is valid only for the stated scope and location. A change of scope needs a new or amended permit before work starts.

lessons.title: Risk levels, WCF and JHA
body: Every permit request starts with a risk rating of Low, Medium or High. The rating decides what paperwork is needed. Low-risk work needs a Work Clearance Form (WCF) only. Medium and High-risk work needs the WCF plus a Job Hazard Analysis (JHA, also called a Risk Assessment). High-risk work additionally runs under a full Permit to Work.

A JHA breaks the job into steps, identifies the hazards in each step, and records the controls that will reduce each risk to an acceptable level. It is prepared by the Permit Holder with the crew who will actually do the work.

Controls are chosen using the hierarchy of controls, most effective first: eliminate the hazard, substitute something less hazardous, use engineering controls (isolation, guarding, ventilation), use administrative controls (procedures, permits, signage), and finally PPE. PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.
The WCF and JHA are completed on site, signed, and uploaded with the permit request so the Permit Issuer can review them.
keyPoints: Low = WCF. Medium/High = WCF + JHA. High also needs a full PTW.
The JHA is step by step: task, hazard, control.
Hierarchy of controls: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administer, PPE.

quiz.prompt: A job has been rated Medium risk. Which documents must be uploaded?
options: No documents are needed for Medium risk
quiz.explanation: Medium and High risk work need both the Work Clearance Form and the Job Hazard Analysis.

quiz.prompt: In the hierarchy of controls, which is the LEAST effective?
quiz.explanation: PPE only protects the person wearing it and relies on correct use, so it is the last line of defence.

quiz.prompt: Who should prepare the JHA?
options: The Permit Holder together with the crew doing the work
Head office, before the site is visited
Anyone, as long as it is signed
quiz.explanation: The people doing the job know the steps best, so the Permit Holder prepares the JHA with the crew.

quiz.prompt: Installing a temporary extraction fan to remove vapour is an example of which type of control?
quiz.explanation: Ventilation physically changes the environment to reduce the hazard, so it is an engineering control.

lessons.title: Isolation, gas testing and close-out
body: Before working on equipment, isolate all energy sources: electrical, mechanical, and the fuel itself. Isolations are locked and tagged (Lock Out, Tag Out, or LOTO) so they cannot be removed while work is in progress. Each worker applies their own personal lock.

Before hot work and before opening any fuel system, the atmosphere must be gas tested with a calibrated detector. Hot work only proceeds when no flammable atmosphere is detected (0 % LEL) in and around the work area. Testing is repeated at the intervals stated on the permit, and continuously where the permit requires it.
If conditions change, for example a tanker arrives, the alarm sounds, or the gas reading rises, stop work and suspend the permit. Work only resumes when the Permit Issuer has re-checked conditions.

When the job is finished, the Permit Holder confirms the site is clean and safe, isolations are removed in the correct order, and the permit is handed back and closed out with the Permit Issuer and Station Manager.
keyPoints: Lock Out, Tag Out (LOTO): every worker applies their own lock.
Hot work needs 0 % LEL in and around the work area.
Changed conditions mean stop work and suspend the permit.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of each worker applying their own personal lock during LOTO?
options: To keep track of who owns which tools
It is only needed for electrical work
To make sure equipment cannot be re-energised until every worker is clear
quiz.explanation: Personal locks mean equipment cannot be re-energised until every individual has removed their own lock, so no one is left exposed.

quiz.prompt: You are about to start grinding. The gas detector reads 4 % LEL at the work point. What do you do?
options: Switch off the detector to stop the alarm
Do not start; hot work requires no flammable atmosphere to be detected
quiz.explanation: Hot work only proceeds when no flammable vapour is detected (0 % LEL). Any reading means the source must be found and controlled first.

quiz.prompt: A fuel tanker arrives to make a delivery while your hot work permit is live. What should happen?
options: Continue, as the tanker driver is responsible for the delivery
Stop work and suspend the permit until conditions are re-checked
Move the work a few metres away and carry on
Ask the tanker to deliver faster
quiz.explanation: A delivery changes site conditions significantly. Work stops and the permit is suspended until the Permit Issuer re-assesses.

quiz.prompt: Who formally closes out the permit when work is complete?
options: The Permit Holder alone, by throwing it away
The Permit Holder hands it back to the Permit Issuer and Station Manager
The first customer to use the pump
quiz.explanation: Close-out is a joint step: the Permit Holder confirms the site is safe and hands the permit back to the Issuer, with the Station Manager informed.

lessons.title: Start-Work Checks: Isolation of Hazardous Energy
body: These are the Start-Work Checks for Isolation of Hazardous Energy: the Save Your Life Actions that must be in place before this work begins. Start Work Authority means "I will not start work until I confirm" every action below.

Every person exposed to the work confirms each action, and the Start-Work Verifier confirms them too. If any safeguard is not in place, stop and seek help. The numbers in the illustration match the actions.

1. Isolation points are identified per plan. How to confirm: Use the Equipment Isolation Procedure, P&IDs, or Process Flow Diagrams to physically confirm all isolations are in place and tagged or marked. Confirm crew has physically inspected the equipment for other potential energy sources not previously identified or isolated.
2. Isolation equipment is rated for the energy source. How to confirm: Confirm blinds, spades and skillets are stamped or certified for the pressure rating of the equipment.

3. Isolation devices are set in the identified position per plan. How to confirm: Confirm valves are open or closed per plan. Confirm blinds, spades and skillets are installed per plan. Confirm switchgear or Motor Control Center (MCC) equipment switches are open and locked out.

4. Isolation points are locked and tagged, and keys are controlled by me or my crew supervisor. How to confirm: Confirm locks, tags or securing devices are on isolation points. Confirm keys are in a designated secure location.

5. Equipment is de-energised and tested for residual or stored energy. How to confirm: Ask crew/operations to attempt to start up equipment. Confirm systems (lines, gauges, etc.) have been tested for residual or stored energy by: Opening bleed and vent points to release stored energy. Pressure testing. Air gapping of lines. Confirm gas testing and atmospheric monitoring will occur when opening piping, equipment, etc.

6. Isolation devices are removed per plan. How to confirm: Physically inspect: Equipment to confirm scope of work was completed. Work area to confirm all mechanical, process and electrical isolations were removed. Bleed and vent points to confirm they are closed.

7. All personnel exposed to energy source have been told equipment is ready to be re-energised. How to confirm: Ask work crews in and near the work area if they are aware equipment is ready to be re-energised.
8. Equipment is ready to be put back in service. How to confirm: Ask work crews in and near the work area if they are aware equipment is ready to be put back in service.
In Gemsafety, record these checks in the Start Work Check section, with your verifier, before work starts. The original Start-Work Check form is linked below.
keyPoints: Isolation points are identified per plan.
Isolation equipment is rated for the energy source.
Isolation devices are set in the identified position per plan.
Isolation points are locked and tagged, and keys are controlled by me or my crew supervisor.
Equipment is de-energised and tested for residual or stored energy.
Isolation devices are removed per plan.
All personnel exposed to energy source have been told equipment is ready to be re-energised.
Equipment is ready to be put back in service.

images.caption: Start-Work Checks — Isolation of Hazardous Energy. The numbers match the actions in this lesson.

resources.label: Start-Work Checks form — Isolation of Hazardous Energy (Word)

quiz.prompt: What must be true of blinds, spades and skillets?
options: The same size as the pipe
Stamped or certified for the pressure rating of the equipment
quiz.explanation: Isolation equipment is rated for the energy source: blinds, spades and skillets are stamped or certified for the pressure rating.

quiz.prompt: How is residual or stored energy tested?
options: Try to start the equipment, open bleed and vent points, pressure test, air gap lines
Ask whether it was switched off
quiz.explanation: Attempt a start-up and test lines and gauges by opening bleed/vent points, pressure testing and air gapping.

quiz.prompt: Who controls the keys for isolation locks?
options: Me or my crew supervisor, kept in a designated secure location
quiz.explanation: Locks and tags are on all isolation points and keys are controlled by me or my crew supervisor.

quiz.prompt: Before re-energising, who must be told?
options: All personnel exposed to the energy source
quiz.explanation: Ask the crews in and near the work area if they know the equipment is ready to be re-energised.

quiz.prompt: After the work, what is checked before the equipment is re-energised?
options: Scope completed, all isolations removed per plan, bleed and vent points closed
Only that the tools are packed
quiz.explanation: Physically inspect the equipment, the work area and the bleed and vent points before re-energising.

title: Defensive Driving Basics
summary: Road transport is the biggest single cause of fatalities in our industry. This course covers defensive driving, how a Journey Management Plan works, and what to do when a journey goes wrong.

lessons.title: Defensive driving basics
body: Defensive driving means driving to prevent collisions despite the actions of others and the conditions around you.

Keep a minimum following distance of three seconds behind the vehicle in front, and at least four seconds at night, in rain, fog or dust, or when towing. Pick a fixed point, and when the vehicle ahead passes it, count. If you reach the point before three seconds, drop back.
Every occupant wears a seatbelt on every journey, in every seat. Mobile phones are not used while driving, including hands-free. Obey posted speed limits and the company limit, whichever is lower.

Fatigue kills. Warning signs include yawning, heavy eyes, drifting in the lane, and missing road signs. The only cure is to stop in a safe place and rest. Opening the window or turning up the music does not work.
keyPoints: Three-second gap minimum; four seconds in poor conditions.
Seatbelts for all, no phones while driving.
Fatigue: stop and rest. There is no other fix.

quiz.prompt: What is the minimum following distance in good conditions?
quiz.explanation: Three seconds gives time to perceive and react. Increase to at least four seconds in poor conditions.

quiz.prompt: You are driving in a dust storm. What following distance should you keep?
options: Stay close to follow their lights
It does not matter at low speed
quiz.explanation: Visibility and braking are affected in dust, fog, rain and darkness, so the gap increases to at least four seconds.

quiz.prompt: Which is the only effective remedy for driver fatigue?
options: Stopping in a safe place to rest
Drinking an energy drink and continuing
quiz.explanation: Fresh air, music and caffeine only mask fatigue briefly. Stopping to rest is the only effective remedy.

quiz.prompt: Who must wear a seatbelt?
quiz.explanation: All occupants wear seatbelts on every journey, front and rear.

lessons.title: How a Journey Management Plan works
body: A Journey Management Plan (JMP) is prepared before any business journey that leaves the city or exceeds the distance set by company policy. The first question is always: is this journey necessary? Could it be combined with another trip, done remotely, or postponed to a safer time?

The JMP records who is driving, the vehicle, the route, departure and arrival times, planned rest stops, call-in points, the hazards on the route and the controls for each. It is reviewed and approved by a Journey Manager before departure.

Rest is planned, not optional: a minimum 15-minute break at least every two hours of driving, and no more than 10 hours of driving in a day. Driving between sunset and sunrise outside city limits is not permitted unless a night-driving exemption has been specifically approved.
The driver calls the Journey Manager at departure, at each planned call-in point, and on arrival. These calls are how the Journey Manager knows the journey is on track.
keyPoints: First ask: is the journey necessary?
15-minute rest at least every 2 hours; max 10 hours driving per day.
No night driving outside cities without an approved exemption.

quiz.prompt: What is the first question to ask when planning a journey?
quiz.explanation: The safest journey is the one that is not made. Journey necessity is always assessed first.

quiz.prompt: How often must a driver take a rest break?
options: A 15-minute break at least every 2 hours
quiz.explanation: A planned 15-minute break at least every two hours of driving manages fatigue before it develops.

quiz.prompt: Who approves a Journey Management Plan before departure?
options: Nobody, as it is a record only
quiz.explanation: The Journey Manager reviews the route, timing, hazards and controls and approves the plan before the vehicle leaves.

quiz.prompt: A journey would require driving after sunset outside the city. Without an approved exemption, you should:
options: Drive faster to arrive before dark
Drive in convoy with another car
Turn on the high beams and continue
Re-plan to arrive before sunset or stop overnight
quiz.explanation: Night driving outside city limits is prohibited unless an exemption is approved, so the journey is re-planned.

lessons.title: Pre-trip checks and overdue journeys
body: Before every journey, walk round the vehicle: tyres (including the spare) for pressure, tread and damage; lights and indicators; brakes; fluid levels; mirrors and windscreen; seatbelts. Confirm the first aid kit, fire extinguisher, warning triangle and drinking water are on board, and that the In-Vehicle Monitoring System (IVMS) is working.

The driver also declares they are fit to drive: well rested with at least 7 hours' sleep, not under the influence of alcohol, drugs or drowsy medication, and holding a valid licence and defensive driving certificate.

If a driver misses a call-in, the overdue procedure starts. After 30 minutes the Journey Manager tries to contact the driver and passengers. After 60 minutes without contact, the Journey Manager escalates to the emergency response team and the last known position from the IVMS is used to start a search.

If you break down in a remote area, stay with your vehicle. It is far easier to find than a person on foot, it gives shade, and it carries your water. Place the warning triangle, call the Journey Manager, and wait.
keyPoints: Walk-round check plus first aid kit, extinguisher, triangle, water, IVMS.
Overdue: 30 minutes, then contact attempts; 60 minutes, then escalate.
Broken down in a remote area: stay with the vehicle.

quiz.prompt: A driver is 30 minutes past a planned call-in with no contact. What does the Journey Manager do?
options: Wait until the end of the day
Start trying to contact the driver and passengers
quiz.explanation: At 30 minutes overdue the Journey Manager actively tries to contact the driver and passengers.

quiz.prompt: After 60 minutes overdue with no contact, the Journey Manager should:
options: Escalate to the emergency response team using the last known IVMS position
quiz.explanation: At 60 minutes without contact the situation is treated as an emergency and escalated, using IVMS data to locate the vehicle.

quiz.prompt: Your vehicle breaks down on a remote desert road. What should you do?
options: Stay with the vehicle, place the warning triangle and call the Journey Manager
Walk to the nearest town for help
Flag down any passing vehicle and leave with them
Try to fix the engine regardless of your experience
quiz.explanation: A vehicle is easier to find than a person, provides shade and holds your water. Stay with it and call in.

quiz.prompt: Which item is part of the driver fitness declaration?
options: At least 7 hours' sleep before the journey
quiz.explanation: Fitness to drive covers rest, freedom from impairment, and valid licence and training.

lessons.title: Start-Work Checks: Heavy Equipment and Vehicle Operations
body: These are the Start-Work Checks for heavy equipment and vehicle operations: the Save Your Life Actions that must be in place before this work begins. Start Work Authority means "I will not start work until I confirm" every action below.

Every person exposed to the work confirms each action, and the Start-Work Verifier confirms them too. If any safeguard is not in place, stop and seek help. The numbers in the illustration match the actions.

1. Controls are in place to segregate pedestrians from mobile equipment and vehicle roadways. How to confirm: A plan to segregate mobile equipment and vehicle roadways from pedestrians is in place. Personnel involved with the activity understand the plan requirements.

2. Vehicle / Equipment is properly certified for duty, and daily inspections are completed and recorded. How to confirm: Equipment is certified to regulatory requirements and maintenance is up to date. Equipment has been inspected in accordance with a quarterly inspection programme. A daily inspection has been completed and recorded by equipment operator. Pre-mobilisation survey is conducted for newly hired equipment. All installed safety devices are working. Operators check for equipment maintenance / lock-out tags. Operators check and wear appropriate PPE and restraints including seat belts.

3. Loads are assessed for stability, securement and capacity for the vehicle / equipment being used. How to confirm: Loads have been assessed for stability, securing, and capacity compatibility with the equipment that will be used.

4. An authorised and competent person is assigned to aid in control of vehicle / equipment movement as required (i.e. flagman, banksman, spotter). How to confirm: An authorised and competent person has been assigned to control equipment movement (i.e. flagger). The flagger and operator have an agreed method of communicating during operation of equipment. Flagger(s) in control of the equipment movement are easily identified. Activity supervisors and flaggers are in place to keep people out of the line of fire during equipment movement.

5. Blind-spots are identified and mitigated, and controls are in place to minimise and manage all equipment and vehicle reversing. How to confirm: Alternatives to reversing have been assessed and eliminated prior to allowing reverse operation of equipment. Audible warnings are working on equipment for reverse operations. Flaggers are positioned out of the line of fire and in a position to monitor reversing operations. Physical barriers are in place in accordance with the activity plan.

6. Controls are in place to manage proximity of equipment and vehicles from excavations, overhead lines, and underground infrastructure. How to confirm: Equipment should be working at the safe distance established for any excavations. Equipment should be working at the safe operational distance established for any overhead powerlines. Equipment should be working at the safe distance established for any underground infrastructure. Minimum Approach Distances (MAD) in HSSE CF Electrical Safety Guide.

7. Vehicles / Equipment are positioned with conditions and controls in place to prevent unintentional movement. How to confirm: Equipment is positioned on flat ground where possible and vehicle wheels are chocked when there is potential for movement. Equipment is positioned in dedicated parking areas, and in accordance with OEM instructions. Booms, attachments and accessories are lowered or secured to prevent energy release.
In Gemsafety, record these checks in the Start Work Check section, with your verifier, before work starts. The original Start-Work Check form is linked below.
keyPoints: Controls are in place to segregate pedestrians from mobile equipment and vehicle roadways.
Vehicle / Equipment is properly certified for duty, and daily inspections are completed and recorded.
Loads are assessed for stability, securement and capacity for the vehicle / equipment being used.
An authorised and competent person is assigned to aid in control of vehicle / equipment movement as required (i.e. flagman, banksman, spotter).
Blind-spots are identified and mitigated, and controls are in place to minimise and manage all equipment and vehicle reversing.
Controls are in place to manage proximity of equipment and vehicles from excavations, overhead lines, and underground infrastructure.
Vehicles / Equipment are positioned with conditions and controls in place to prevent unintentional movement.

quiz.prompt: What must happen before a vehicle is allowed to reverse?
options: Alternatives to reversing are assessed and eliminated first
quiz.explanation: Alternatives to reversing are assessed and eliminated before reverse operation is allowed.

quiz.prompt: Who controls vehicle and equipment movement where needed?
options: An authorised, competent flagman / banksman / spotter
quiz.explanation: An authorised and competent person is assigned to control movement, with an agreed way of communicating with the operator.

quiz.prompt: Who completes and records the daily inspection?
quiz.explanation: A daily inspection is completed and recorded by the equipment operator, alongside the quarterly programme.

quiz.prompt: How is parked equipment prevented from moving?
options: Flat ground where possible, wheels chocked, booms and attachments lowered
quiz.explanation: Equipment is on flat ground, wheels chocked when needed, and booms and attachments lowered or secured.

quiz.prompt: How are pedestrians protected?
options: Segregated from mobile equipment and vehicle roadways by a plan
quiz.explanation: Controls segregate pedestrians from mobile equipment and vehicle roadways.

title: Fire Response Basics
summary: An optional refresher on how fires start, which extinguisher to use on which class of fire, and when to fight a fire or leave.

lessons.title: Fire classes and extinguishers
body: A fire needs three things: fuel, heat and oxygen. This is the fire triangle. Remove any one and the fire goes out. Extinguishers work by cooling (removing heat), smothering (removing oxygen) or interrupting the chemical reaction.

Fires are grouped by what is burning. Class A is ordinary solids such as paper, wood and fabric. Class B is flammable liquids such as petrol and diesel. Class C is flammable gases such as LPG. Class D is burning metals. Electrical fires involve live equipment. Class F is cooking oils and fats.

Water extinguishers are for Class A only. Foam covers Class A and B. Dry powder (ABC) covers A, B and C and is the most common extinguisher on forecourts. CO2 is used on electrical fires and small Class B fires and leaves no residue.
keyPoints: Fire triangle: fuel, heat, oxygen.
Class B = flammable liquids (petrol, diesel).
CO2 for electrical fires; never water on live equipment.

quiz.prompt: What are the three sides of the fire triangle?
quiz.explanation: A fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen. Removing any one extinguishes it.

quiz.prompt: A fire involving diesel is which class?
quiz.explanation: Class B fires involve flammable liquids such as petrol and diesel.

quiz.prompt: Which extinguisher is most suitable for a fire in a live electrical panel?
quiz.explanation: CO2 does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue, making it suitable for electrical fires.

lessons.title: Using an extinguisher safely
body: Use the PASS technique: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side.

Before you fight a fire, ask: has the alarm been raised? Is the fire small and contained? Do I have the right extinguisher? Is my escape route behind me and clear? If the answer to any of these is no, leave and let the emergency services deal with it.
Never turn your back on a fire you have just put out; it can re-ignite. Back away while watching it.
keyPoints: PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.
Alarm raised, fire small, right extinguisher, escape route clear, otherwise leave.
Back away from an extinguished fire.

quiz.prompt: In the PASS technique, where should you aim the extinguisher?
options: At the top of the flames
Into the air above the fire
At the base of the fire
quiz.explanation: Aiming at the base attacks the fuel that is burning, not just the flames.

quiz.prompt: When should you NOT attempt to fight a fire?
options: When it is small and you have the right extinguisher
When your escape route is blocked or the fire is spreading
When the alarm has been raised
quiz.explanation: If the fire is large or spreading, or your escape route is not clear, leave and let the emergency services handle it.

quiz.prompt: After putting out a small fire, you should:
options: Touch it to check it is cold
Back away while continuing to watch it
quiz.explanation: Fires can re-ignite. Back away facing the fire so you can react.
